title: Correlation & Regression
subtitle: Contact session 11 · slides CS-11 · covariance, Pearson's r, autocovariance, autocorrelation, PCA, regression, r², Spearman

lesson.title: Why this matters in AI and ML
lesson.lead: Before you model anything, you ask: do these two things move together? Covariance and correlation answer that.

blocks.text: Where you will meet these ideas

items: **Feature selection:** two input features with a correlation near +1 or −1 carry almost the same information.
**Regression:** the slope of a fitted line is built from a covariance (slide 13).
**PCA:** diagonalising the covariance matrix gives the principal components (slides 15–16).
**Time series:** autocovariance and autocorrelation compare a series with a shifted copy of itself (slides 13–14, then CS 13).

blocks.text: Slides 3–5: one variable or two?

head: Situation
What you need
rows: Descriptive statistics are enough: mean, variance, standard deviation.
Two or more variables (Showtime revenue vs advertising, example 2)
Summaries are not enough. You also need to know whether the variables are related.

blocks.label: Plan for this chapter
blocks.text: Covariance first (it is the raw measure), then Pearson's r (covariance made unit-free), then autocovariance and autocorrelation, then PCA as an application. Regression, r² and Spearman come next in this chapter.

lesson.title: Covariance from data (slides 6–8)
lesson.lead: Covariance tells you the direction of the linear relationship between two variables. It does not tell you the strength.

blocks.text: The idea

Take each point and ask two questions: is X above or below its average, and is Y above or below its average? If both are above, or both are below, the product of the two gaps is positive. If they disagree, the product is negative. Add up the products. The total tells you which kind of point wins.

blocks.caption: slide 8 (written there for X1 and X2)

head: Sign of Cov
Meaning
rows: X and Y tend to move in the same direction
X and Y tend to move in opposite directions

blocks.text: Standard steps

items: Count the pairs: n.
Find X̄ and Ȳ.
Subtract the mean from every X and every Y (deviations).
Multiply the two deviations in each row.
Add the products.
Divide by n − 1 (sample covariance).
Read the sign and say what it means.

blocks.text: What covariance cannot do (slide 7)

items: Its value can be any real number, from minus infinity to plus infinity.
Its size depends on the units: change kg to grams and the number changes. So the size says nothing about strength.
Its limits depend on the variances of X and Y, which depend on the scales.
Only the sign is meaningful. That is the reason Pearson's r was invented.

blocks.label: Check yourself
blocks.text: The deviations X − X̄ always add up to 0, and so do the Y − Ȳ. If yours do not, a mean is wrong.

lesson.title: The slide's covariance example (slides 10–11)
lesson.lead: Age and weight of six children: Cov = 10.6, positive.

items: Deviations X − X̄: −2, −3, 0, 3, 1, 1. Deviations Y − Ȳ: −4, −6, −1, 8, 2, 1.
Sum of products = 53.
Positive: older children weigh more.

blocks.label: Slide quirk
blocks.text: The slide's table uses Ȳ = 23, which gives Y deviations −3, −5, 0, 9, 3, 2. The true mean is 24. The products then differ row by row but the total is still **53**, because the X deviations add to 0. Write Ȳ = 24 in the exam and you still get 53 and 10.6.

lesson.title: Covariance from a probability table (slide 12)
lesson.lead: When the question gives probabilities instead of data values, use expectations.

blocks.text: If X and Y are random variables with a probability mass function p(x) or density f(x), the slide gives:
Cov(X, Y) = E[(X − μX)(Y − μY)] = E(XY) − E(X) E(Y)
blocks.caption: slide 12, where E(X) = μX and E(Y) = μY

head: The question gives
Use
rows: A joint probability table, pmf or pdf

blocks.text: Standard steps

items: Check the table adds to 1.
Add across rows and down columns to get the separate probabilities of X and of Y.
E(X) = Σ x·P(x).
E(Y) = Σ y·P(y).
E(XY) = Σ x·y·p(x, y) over every cell.
Cov = E(XY) − E(X)E(Y).
Interpret the sign.

blocks.label: Add-on (not on the slides)
blocks.text: If X and Y are independent, E(XY) = E(X)E(Y), so Cov = 0. The reverse is not always true: Cov = 0 only means no *linear* relationship. To prove independence you must check p(x, y) = P(x)·P(y) in **every** cell. A nonzero covariance does prove they are dependent.

blocks.label: Common mistake
blocks.text: No division by n − 1 here. The probabilities already add to 1 and act as the weights.

lesson.title: Variance-covariance matrix and applications (slides 9, 13–16)
lesson.lead: Put every variance and covariance in one square table. Then use it for regression, time series and PCA.

blocks.text: The matrix (slide 9)
For n variables, the variance-covariance matrix has the variances on the diagonal and the covariances off the diagonal. It is symmetric, because Cov(X, Y) = Cov(Y, X).
For the age and weight data: Var(X) = 24/5 = 4.8, Var(Y) = 122/5 = 24.4 and Cov = 10.6 (my calculation from the slide data).
Three applications

items: **Multivariate linear regression (slide 13):** with one dependent variable and several independent ones, the variance-covariance matrix describes how they relate. The professor added that the regression coefficient is built from a covariance.
**Time series (slides 13–14):** a series is a set of random variables, one per time point. Autocovariance is the covariance between two of them (next boards).
**PCA (slides 15–16):** see the board after Pearson's r.

lesson.title: Pearson's correlation coefficient r (slides 17–22)
lesson.lead: Divide the covariance by both standard deviations. The units cancel and r always lies between −1 and +1.

blocks.text: Karl Pearson's idea (slide 17): divide the covariance of the variables by their standard deviations. The result is the product moment correlation, written r. It is free of units and measures the strength **and** direction of the relationship between two continuous variables.

blocks.caption: covariance divided by both standard deviations, s_{X} = √Var(X) (slides 17–19)

blocks.text: Work it as covariance over the standard deviations. Compute Cov(X, Y), Var(X) and Var(Y), take the square roots, then divide. The n − 1 cancels out of the top and bottom, so Σ(X − X̄)(Y − Ȳ) / √[Σ(X − X̄)² · Σ(Y − Ȳ)²] gives the same r. The slides' sums form (five column totals) is an equal alternative that you can use as a check.
Strength table (slide 22)
The sign gives the direction: positive means a direct relationship (both rise together), negative means an inverse relationship (one rises while the other falls) (slide 20).
Standard steps

items: Count the pairs: n. Find X̄ and Ȳ.
Deviations X − X̄ and Y − Ȳ.
Cov(X, Y) = Σ(X − X̄)(Y − Ȳ) / (n − 1). Its sign is the sign of r.
Var(X) = Σ(X − X̄)² / (n − 1) and s_{X} = √Var(X). Same for Y.
r = Cov(X, Y) / (s_{X} · s_{Y}).
Check with the slides' sums form: nΣXY − ΣX·ΣY over √[(nΣX² − (ΣX)²)(nΣY² − (ΣY)²)].
Write the sign, the strength word from the table, and one sentence in the words of the problem.

blocks.label: Self-check
blocks.text: r can never be above +1 or below −1. If you get 1.4, recheck ΣX², ΣY² and (ΣX)². Do not confuse ΣX² (square each, then add) with (ΣX)² (add, then square).

lesson.title: Autocovariance (slides 13–14)
lesson.lead: The covariance of a time series with a shifted copy of itself. The shift is called the lag h.

blocks.text: A time series is a set of random variables, one for every time point. Autocovariance asks how the value at time t varies together with the value at time t + h. The slide defines it as a covariance:
autocovariance at lag h = Cov( X_{t+h} , X_{t} )
blocks.caption: slide 13

blocks.text: For observed data X(t1), X(t2), ..., X(tn), the slide gives the sample version:

blocks.caption: slide 14. The sum runs over i = 1 to n − |h|, for −n < h < n

blocks.label: Professor's lecture (25 Oct)
blocks.text: He pointed out a typo in the slide's formula: the index that runs inside the sum is **i**, not t, so the sum is over i = 1 to n − |h|. He also stressed that this is a **sample** autocovariance, computed from your observations, which only approximates the true value.
In plain words

items: Find X̄, the mean of all n values.
Subtract X̄ from every value to get deviations.
For lag h, pair each deviation with the deviation h positions later.
Multiply each pair and add the products. There are n − h pairs.
Divide by **n** (not n − h and not n − 1).

blocks.text: Facts to remember

items: Lag 0 pairs every deviation with itself, so γ̂(0) is the variance of the series (divided by n).
A positive γ̂(h) means that values h steps apart tend to be on the same side of the average.
For a stationary series the autocovariance depends only on the lag h, not on where in the series you start (CS 13).

blocks.label: Common mistake
blocks.text: Do not divide by n − 1 here. The slide formula divides by n, in the covariance-of-a-series style.

lesson.title: Autocorrelation (slide 14, then CS 13 slides 10–12)
lesson.lead: Autocovariance made unit-free by dividing by the variation of the series.

blocks.text: Autocorrelation measures how strongly a series at the current time is related to its own earlier values (CS 13, slide 10). The slide gives:

blocks.caption: slide 14. Top: sum over t = k + 1 to T. Bottom: sum over t = 1 to T

blocks.text: CS 13 slide 12 writes the same thing for k = 1, 2, ...: r_{1} pairs y_{t} with y_{t−1}, r_{2} pairs y_{t} with y_{t−2}, and so on.

items: The numerator has T − k products. The denominator has T squares.
r_{k} always lies between −1 and +1, like Pearson's r.
r_{0} = 1, because a series is perfectly correlated with itself.
Because both the autocovariance and the denominator here are divided by n in the same way, r_{k} = γ̂(k) / γ̂(0). That gives you a check.
The professor described autocorrelation as the numerator of the autocovariance divided by what looks like a variance of the series.

blocks.label: Where this goes next
blocks.text: CS 13 uses these to decide whether a series is genuinely dependent on its past or just random noise, and to choose AR and MA models. We will compute them on the retail sales table in CS 13 (slide 13).

lesson.title: PCA: covariance in action (slides 15–16)
lesson.lead: Principal components come from the eigenvectors of the variance-covariance matrix.

items: PCA is often described as "diagonalizing the covariance matrix" (slide 15). That means finding a combination of the original variables that makes the covariance matrix diagonal.
When this is done the new variables are uncorrelated. These combinations are called principal components.
Let A be the variance-covariance matrix. The components come from the eigenvalue problem A x = λ x, where λ is an eigenvalue and x is the matching eigenvector.

A large eigenvalue means the matching principal component is important in describing the data (slide 16). An eigenvalue near zero means the component is relatively unimportant, so the data depend mainly on fewer components.

blocks.label: Professor's lecture (25 Oct)
blocks.text: The eigenvectors give the principal component directions and the eigenvalues give the strength along them. He noted this is also being learned in MFML, so it is a definition-level topic here.

blocks.label: Wording
blocks.text: The slide says the uncorrelated variables are "independent". Uncorrelated only means zero linear relationship. Be careful with the word independent in your own answers.

lesson.title: Regression: the idea (slides 39–42)
lesson.lead: Predict Y from X with a straight line. Y is the thing you predict, X is what you use to predict it.

blocks.text: The Showtime movie-theatre owner wants to predict weekly gross revenue (Y) from television advertising (X) (slide 39). Build the model in three steps:

items: Simplest guess: revenue is proportional to advertising, **Y = bX**.

But revenue is not zero when there is no advertising, so add an intercept: **Y = a + bX**. Here **a** is the baseline revenue at X = 0 and **b** is the slope, the expected change in revenue for one extra unit of advertising.
Real measurements also contain randomness, so the full model is **Y = a + bX + ε** (slide 40). This is the simple linear regression model.

head: Name
Also called
rows: dependent variable, response variable, predicted variable
independent variable, explanatory variable, predictor variable

blocks.text: Assumptions about the error ε (slide 42)

items: ε is a random variable with mean 0.
Its variance σ² is the same for every value of X.
The values of ε are independent.
ε is normally distributed.

blocks.label: Professor's lecture (25 Oct)
blocks.text: The slides use the symbol ε both for the model's noise and for the gap between an actual and a fitted value. He solved the fitting as a plain curve-fitting (deterministic) problem and said the same a and b are also the best values for the noisy model.

lesson.title: Least squares and the formulas (slides 43–46)
lesson.lead: Choose the line that makes the total squared error as small as possible.

items: For a candidate line, the **residual** of each point is actual Y minus predicted Ŷ.
Square each residual, so positive and negative errors cannot cancel, and add them: Σ(Y − a − bX)².
Find the a and b that make this smallest: set the derivative with respect to a to 0, then with respect to b to 0 (slide 44).
That gives two equations, the **normal equations** (slide 45).
Solving them gives the formulas for b̂ and â (slide 46).

blocks.text:
ΣY = n·a + b·ΣX          (1)
ΣXY = a·ΣX + b·ΣX²          (2)
blocks.caption: the normal equations

blocks.text: b̂ = {{ Cov(X, Y) // Var(X) }}  =  {{ Σ(X − X̄)(Y − Ȳ) // Σ(X − X̄)² }}  =  {{ nΣXY − (ΣX)(ΣY) // nΣX² − (ΣX)² }}
blocks.caption: slope: the two forms are equal. The professor's reading: sample covariance of X and Y divided by the sample variance of X

blocks.text: â = Ȳ − b̂ · X̄
Ŷ = â + b̂ · X
blocks.caption: the fitted regression model

blocks.label: Do you need the derivation?
blocks.text: No. In the six end-sem papers I checked, every regression question was numeric (fit, predict, interpret). It is open book. Know the two normal equations and the final formulas, and the one-line reason: minimise the sum of squared errors.

blocks.label: Common mistake
blocks.text: The denominator uses the **X** deviations, Σ(X − X̄)². Do not use the Y deviations. The Showtime slide makes exactly this slip (see the Showtime board).

lesson.title: Regression: standard steps and keywords
lesson.lead: The same nine steps every time, and the words that tell you it is regression.

blocks.text: Standard steps

items: Decide X and Y. The variable you predict, or the "effect on" variable, is Y.
Write the formulas first.
n, X̄ and Ȳ.
Deviations x = X − X̄ and y = Y − Ȳ. Each list must add to 0.
Columns xy and x². Add them: Σxy and Σx².
Slope b̂ = Σxy / Σx².
Intercept â = Ȳ − b̂·X̄.
Write the line Ŷ = â + b̂X, then substitute any X they ask about.
Write one sentence: direction, size with units, and the prediction.

blocks.label: Check
blocks.text: The fitted line always passes through (X̄, Ȳ). If they ask for a prediction at X = X̄, the answer must be Ȳ.
Keywords: how you know it is regression

head: Words in the question
What you do
rows: "effect of A on B", "predict B based on A", "Y = f(X)"
A is X, B is Y
"fit a line", "least squares", "SSE as the loss", "simple regression model", "find a suitable linear relation"
b̂, â, then Ŷ = â + b̂X
Sign of b̂ in the words of the problem
"check whether x and y have a linear relation", "coefficient of correlation"
Plot the points, then the line
"is the linear model appropriate?", "what does the pattern suggest", "optimal range"
Judge from the plot and residuals (Feb 2026)
"coefficient of determination", "variation explained", "how good is the fit"

blocks.text: Interpretation sentence

"The slope is **[positive/negative]**, so **[Y]** **[increases/decreases]** as **[X]** increases. Each extra **[unit of X]** changes **[Y]** by about **[b̂]** **[unit of Y]**. At **[X value]** the predicted **[Y]** is **[Ŷ]**."

Example: "The slope is positive, so extraction efficiency increases with extraction time. Each extra minute raises efficiency by about 0.76 percentage points. At 35 minutes the predicted efficiency is about 65.8%."

lesson.title: Slide example: Showtime (slides 47–49) and its error
lesson.lead: The slide's table has its x and y column headings swapped, so the printed slope 0.407 is wrong. The correct slope is 1.604.

blocks.text: **The problem (slide 47):** The owner of a Showtime movie theatre wishes to predict weekly gross revenue based on advertising expenditures. The sample data are as follows.
What the slide does (slides 48–49)
It prints Σxy = 10.375 and Σx² = 25.5, then b̂ = 10.375 / 25.5 = 0.407, â = 92.45 and Ŷ = 92.45 + 0.407X, giving 94.28 at X = 4.5. The professor repeated this in the lecture.

blocks.label: The error
blocks.text: In the slide-48 table the column headed x = (X − X̄) actually holds the **Y** deviations (96 − 93.75 = 2.25), and the column headed y holds the **X** deviations (5.0 − 3.19 = 1.81). So "Σx² = 25.5" is the sum of squared **Y** deviations. The formula on slide 46 is right, but the denominator must use the **X** deviations.
The correct working

items: Σx² (X deviations) = ΣX² − (ΣX)²/n = 87.75 − 81.28 = **6.469**.

blocks.text: Sense check: at X = 4 the correct line gives 95.05 and the data say 95. The slide's line gives 94.08 at X = 4 and 93.26 at X = 2, where the data say 90.

lesson.title: r²: how good is the line? (slides 50–59)
lesson.lead: The fraction of the total variation in Y that the regression line explains.

blocks.text: After fitting the line, slide 50 asks: how good is it? Split the total variation in Y into the part the line explains and the part it leaves over.

SST = Σ(Y − Ȳ)²          total variation (slide 51)
SSR = Σ(Ŷ − Ȳ)²          explained by the line (slide 52)
SSE = Σ(Y − Ŷ)²          error left over (slide 53)
SST = SSR + SSE
blocks.caption: slide 54

blocks.text: r² = {{ SSR // SST }} = {{ Σ(Ŷ − Ȳ)² // Σ(Y − Ȳ)² }}
blocks.caption: slide 55. Always between 0 and 1

blocks.label: Same thing, other way round
blocks.text: Since SST = SSR + SSE, also r² = 1 − SSE / SST. Use this when SSE and SST are given (practice problem 4.5).
Standard steps

items: Fit the line first.
Compute Ŷ for every X.
SST = Σ(Y − Ȳ)².
SSR = Σ(Ŷ − Ȳ)².
r² = SSR / SST.
Check: SSE = SST − SSR should equal Σ(Y − Ŷ)².
Say it in words.

blocks.text: The slide example (slides 56–59)
Number of TV advertisements X = 1, 3, 2, 1, 3, 2 and number of cars sold Y = 14, 24, 18, 17, 27, 20. Fit a regression line of Y on X and find the coefficient of determination.

Interpretation (slide 59): about 87.7% of the variability in the number of cars sold is explained by the linear regression on TV advertisements. The remaining 12.3% is due to other factors or random variation.

blocks.label: Add-on (not on the slides)
blocks.text: r² equals the square of Pearson's r. So r = + or − √r², with the sign of the slope b̂. Here r = +0.937.

blocks.label: Slide note
blocks.text: The slide-57 table lists only five of the six data pairs. The missing pair (2, 20) adds 0 to every column, so the results are the same.

lesson.title: Spearman's rank correlation (add-on)
lesson.lead: Pearson's r computed on ranks. Asked once, in May 2026 (5 marks).

blocks.label: Where it comes from
blocks.text: The slides only name it (slide 18) and the professor said it would not be covered. But the 23 May 2026 paper asked it for 5 marks, so it is worth fifteen minutes. The textbooks cover it: T1 Kaptein §6.6.3, R1 Miller & Freund §14.4, R2 Anderson et al. §19.5 (equation 19.8).
Use it when the data are **ranks** (judges, orderings) or when the question says **rank correlation**. It measures how well two orderings agree: +1 identical, −1 exactly opposite, 0 no agreement.
Step 1: get the ranks
If the problem already gives ranks, go to step 2. If it gives raw values (marks, scores, sales), rank each column separately:

items: Sort the column from smallest to largest and number the positions 1, 2, 3, …
The smallest value gets rank 1. Rank **both** columns in the same direction (smallest = 1 in both, or largest = 1 in both).
A value that repeats is a **tie**: give each tied value the **average** of the positions they occupy. Two values at positions 3 and 4 both get 3.5. Three values at positions 2, 3, 4 each get 3.
The next value carries on from the last position used, so after the three 75s at positions 2 to 4 the next rank is 5 and rank 4 is never used.
Check: the ranks of each column add to n(n + 1)/2.

blocks.text: Step 2: decide the method by scanning for ties
Look down each column of ranks (or raw values) for a repeated number. **Repeats inside the same column** are ties. The same number appearing in X and in Y is not a tie.

head: What you see
Method
rows: Ranks given, no repeats in either column
Raw values, nothing repeats in either column: rank, then
Raw values with a repeat in X or in Y: rank with averages, then

blocks.text: You do not need both methods. The d² formula is the quick route and it is exact only when there are no ties. The covariance method always works, so use it whenever there is a tie.
Method A: no ties, the d² formula (R2 equation 19.8)

blocks.caption: d = rank of X − rank of Y

items: Write d for each pair; the d column adds to 0.
Square: d². Add: Σd².
Substitute n and Σd².
Conclusion: sign for direction, size for strength.

blocks.text: Method B: ties, the covariance method (T1 §6.6.3, R1 §14.4)
r_{s} = {{ Cov(rank X, rank Y) // s_{X} · s_{Y} }}
blocks.caption: Pearson's r computed on the ranks

items: Mean rank = (n + 1)/2.
Table: rank X − mean, rank Y − mean, their product, and the two squares. Add each column.
Cov = Σ product / (n − 1). Var = Σ square / (n − 1), then s = √Var.
Conclusion.

blocks.label: The symbol
blocks.text: Pearson's formula on ranks gives the Spearman coefficient, written r_{s}. In the exam you may write "Pearson's r on the ranks = r_{s}".
The four scenarios

head: Scenario
Example in the Classroom
Route
rows: Test marks; ties in both columns

blocks.text: May 2026, Q4 (5 marks), a ranks-with-ties case
Two judges ranked 6 products. Judge A: 1, 2, 3.5, 3.5, 5, 6. Judge B: 2, 1, 4, 3, 6, 5. Find Spearman's rank correlation coefficient and give your conclusion.

A has a 3.5 twice, so there are ties: covariance method. Σxy = 15, Σx² = 17, Σy² = 17.5, so r_{s} = 15 / √(17 × 17.5) = **0.87**. The d² formula would give 0.871, which is close but only approximate here.
**Textbook example (Anderson et al., Table 19.16):** 10 salespeople ranked on potential and on later sales, with no ties. Σd² = 44 and n = 10, so r_{s} = 1 − 6(44)/990 = **0.733**.

blocks.label: Common mistakes
blocks.text: Counting the same number in X and Y as a tie. Ranking one column smallest-first and the other largest-first. Forgetting to average tied ranks. Using d² when there are ties. Dropping the conclusion sentence.

lesson.title: Appropriateness, extrapolation and choosing a model
lesson.lead: The judgement parts of regression questions: 1 to 3 marks each.

blocks.text: Is a straight line appropriate? (Feb 2026, Q5 ii)

items: Plot Y against X. Do the points follow a straight band?
Look at the residuals Y − Ŷ. If they are negative at both ends and positive in the middle (or the reverse), the data curve and a straight line is only an approximation.
A high r² says the line explains much of the variation, but not that it is the best shape.

blocks.text: Extrapolation (2023 makeup Q4)
The data had X from 9 to 14, but the question asked for a prediction at x = 20. Compute it, then add: "x = 20 is outside the observed range, so the prediction is less reliable."
Choosing between regression models (2023 end-sem Q4b, 3 marks)

Team A: multiple linear regression with SSE as the loss, accuracy 80%. Team B: polynomial regression with SSE, accuracy 90%. Team C: multiple regression fitted by gradient descent, accuracy 85%. Write your observations and pick the best model.

blocks.label: Add-on reasoning (not in the slides)
blocks.text: A and C are the same kind of model (a linear model that minimises SSE). Gradient descent is just a way of finding the same solution, so the difference between 80% and 85% comes from how well it was trained or tuned. B has the highest accuracy but a polynomial is more flexible and can overfit, so check accuracy on data not used for fitting. Choose B only if its accuracy holds on a test set; otherwise prefer the simpler model.

blocks.label: Wording
blocks.text: Say what you would check, not only the percentages: a held-out test set, model complexity and overfitting.
When the prediction goes beyond the data: two cases

head: Case
What you see
What to write
rows: X is outside the range of the data (2023 makeup: data 9 to 14, asked at x = 20)
Give the number, then say x is outside the observed range, so the prediction is less reliable.
Ŷ cannot happen (a score above 100, a negative count)
Say the line predicts this value but it is impossible, so the linear model does not hold this far outside the data.

blocks.text: Why: the line only describes the pattern in the X values you observed. Real relationships often flatten, as the Feb 2026 water and yield data do at high water input.

items: Do the substitution and give the number.
State that X is outside the observed range, so the prediction is less reliable.
If the value is impossible, say so, and say the relationship probably levels off.

blocks.label: Marks
blocks.text: You lose marks for leaving out the number, not for adding the warning. The warning usually earns the understanding marks.

lesson.title: Which tool? Pearson, Spearman, regression, r², autocorrelation
lesson.lead: Read the question's words and look at the data. That picks the tool; you do not choose by the size of the answer.

head: What the question says or gives
Tool
rows: A probability table of X and Y; "covariance"
Raw measurements; "Karl Pearson", "coefficient of correlation", "linear relation", "strength and direction"
"Fit a line", "least squares", "predict", "effect of A on B"

blocks.text: **Pearson or Spearman?** Pearson uses the actual values and measures how well they follow a straight line. Spearman uses only the order, so it fits data that are rankings. If the question names the method, follow the name; if unsure, marks, measurements and amounts mean Pearson and ranks mean Spearman.

blocks.label: Add-on (not on the slides)
blocks.text: Spearman on raw values is also used when an extreme value distorts Pearson, or when the relationship rises steadily but not in a straight line. Use it only when the question asks for rank correlation.

blocks.label: Past papers
blocks.text: 2024 end-sem Q1a gave marks and said Karl Pearson: Pearson. May 2026 Q4 gave judges' ranks and said rank correlation: Spearman. The same data can be asked several ways (see the All together problem).

blocks.label: Do not choose by the answer
blocks.text: r and r_{s} usually come out close (0.925 and 0.971 in the capstone), but neither is better. Each answers the question that was asked.

blocks.label: Y is a constant: covariance 0, correlation undefined
blocks.text: The slide with the zero-correlation figures suggests that a constant Y gives r = 0. The professor corrected this. worked.title: Auto · Sample autocovariance (practice, my numbers)

problem.text: A series has the values 4, 6, 5, 7, 8. Find the sample autocovariance γ̂(h) for h = 0, 1, 2 using the slide formula.

steps.label: Lag 0
steps.text: Pair each deviation with itself: 4 + 0 + 1 + 1 + 4 = 10. γ̂(0) = 10/5 = **2**.

steps.label: Lag 1
steps.text: Pair each deviation with the next one: (0)(−2) + (−1)(0) + (1)(−1) + (2)(1) = 0 + 0 − 1 + 2 = 1. That is n − 1 = 4 products. γ̂(1) = 1/5 = **0.2**.

steps.label: Lag 2
steps.text: Pair with the one two steps on: (−1)(−2) + (1)(0) + (2)(−1) = 2 + 0 − 2 = 0. That is n − 2 = 3 products. γ̂(2) = 0/5 = **0**.

steps.label: Reading
steps.text: γ̂(0) is the variance of the series. The small positive γ̂(1) says neighbouring values lean slightly the same way; at lag 2 the relationship disappears.

worked.title: Auto · Autocorrelation of the same series (practice)

problem.text: For the series 4, 6, 5, 7, 8, find r_{1} and r_{2} from the slide formula, and check with γ̂(k)/γ̂(0).

steps.label: r1
steps.text: Numerator: Σ over t = 2 to 5 of (y_{t} − ȳ)(y_{t−1} − ȳ) = 1 (from the previous problem). r_{1} = 1/10 = **0.1**.

steps.label: r2
steps.text: Numerator: Σ over t = 3 to 5 of (y_{t} − ȳ)(y_{t−2} − ȳ) = 0. r_{2} = **0**.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: γ̂(1)/γ̂(0) = 0.2/2 = 0.1 and γ̂(2)/γ̂(0) = 0. They agree because both divide by n.

worked.title: Regression · Water input and yield (Feb 2026 Q5)

problem.text: The Mumbai Urban Farming Initiative (MUFI) is piloting IoT-enabled smart irrigation systems in rooftop vegetable gardens across Mumbai. Data were collected from 10 gardens over one growing season. X: average daily water input (L/m²/day). Y: crop yield (kg/m²) for leafy greens. The goal is to model the relationship between water input and yield to optimise resource use and avoid over-irrigation. [2 + 1 + 2 marks]

i. Fit a simple linear regression model Y = β0 + β1X. ii. Discuss whether the linear model is appropriate. What does the pattern suggest? iii. Based on your analysis, what is the optimal water input range (in L/m²/day) for maximising yield per unit water (water-use efficiency)? steps.label: (i) Fit
steps.text: b̂ = 6.354 / 15.529 = **0.409**. â = 2.24 − 0.409 × 3.99 = **0.607**. **Ŷ = 0.607 + 0.409X**. Yield rises by about 0.41 kg/m² for each extra litre per m² per day. r² = 0.895.

steps.label: (ii) Appropriate?
steps.text: r² = 0.895, so a straight line explains most of the variation. But the residuals are negative at both ends (X = 2.0: −0.23, X = 6.0: −0.36) and positive in the middle (X = 4.2: +0.17, X = 5.1: +0.21). That curved pattern says yield has diminishing returns: it flattens at high water input. The line is a good first model, but a curve would fit better.

steps.label: (iii) Optimal range

| 15 | 3 | 2–4 | 3 |
| 25 | 1 | 5 | 5 |
In the original order the ranks are: 1, 3, 3, 3, 5. Check: the ranks add to n(n + 1)/2 = 15; here 15. A value repeats, so this column has ties.

steps.label: Decide the method
steps.text: Scan each column for repeated values. X repeats a value; Y repeats a value. Ties found, so use the covariance method (Pearson on the ranks).

steps.label: Why not d²?
steps.text: With ties the d² formula is only approximate (it would give 0.925). Give the covariance answer.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.text: r_{s} ≈ 0.92: a very strong positive rank correlation.

problem.text: Six students scored 82, 75, 91, 75, 68 and 75. Rank them (smallest = 1).

steps.label: Rank

Sort smallest to largest, number the positions 1 to 6, and give a tied value the average of its positions.
| value | how many | positions | rank |
| 68 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 75 | 3 | 2–4 | 3 |
| 82 | 1 | 5 | 5 |
| 91 | 1 | 6 | 6 |

worked.title: Capstone · Study hours and exam score (all of Chapter 11)

problem.text: Six students recorded their weekly study time and their exam score (out of 100). [Covariance, correlation, regression, r² and rank correlation in one problem.]

(a) Find the covariance of X and Y and say what its sign tells you. (b) Calculate Karl Pearson's coefficient of correlation and interpret it. (c) Fit the regression line of score on study hours by least squares, interpret the slope, and predict the score for 5 hours and for 10 hours. (d) Find the coefficient of determination and interpret it. (e) Find Spearman's rank correlation coefficient.

steps.label: Read the problem
steps.text: Two columns for the same six students, and five different questions. Each question has its own keyword: "covariance" / "direction" → Cov; "Karl Pearson" / "strength" → r; "fit a line" / "predict" → regression; "variation explained" → r²; "rank correlation" → Spearman. Hours of study is the thing used to predict, so X = hours, Y = score.

steps.label: (a) Covariance
steps.text: Cov(X, Y) = Σ(X − X̄)(Y − Ȳ) / (n − 1) = 76 / 5 = **15.2**. Positive, so hours and score move in the same direction. The size alone does not say how strong.

steps.label: (b) Pearson's r
steps.text: Var(X) = 14 / 5 = 2.8, s_{X} = 1.6733. Var(Y) = 482 / 5 = 96.4, s_{Y} = 9.8184. r = Cov / (s_{X} · s_{Y}) = 15.2 / (1.6733 × 9.8184) = **0.925**. Strong positive (0.76 to 0.99, slide 22): students who study more tend to score higher.

steps.label: (c) Regression slope
steps.text: b̂ = Cov(X, Y) / Var(X) = 15.2 / 2.8 = **5.4286**. It equals Σxy / Σx² = 76 / 14, since the n − 1 cancels.

steps.label: (c) Predict
steps.text: At X = 5: Ŷ = 42.2857 + 5.4286 × 5 = **69.43**. At X = 10: Ŷ = 96.57, but 10 hours is outside the data (2 to 6 hours), so this is extrapolation and less reliable. Check: at X = X̄ = 4 the line gives 64 = Ȳ.

steps.label: (c) Sentence
steps.text: The slope is positive, so the score rises with study time: about 5.4 marks for each extra hour. A student who studies 5 hours is predicted to score about 69.4.

steps.label: (d) r²
steps.text: r² = SSR / SST = 412.57 / 482 = **0.856**. Check: SSE = 482 − 412.57 = 69.43, and r² = 1 − 69.43/482 = 0.856, which also equals 0.925². About 85.6% of the variation in scores is explained by study hours; the other 14.4% is other factors or chance.

steps.label: (e) How the ranks came out
steps.text: X ranks: 2 → 1, the two 3s → 2.5, 4 → 4, the two 6s → 5.5 (ties). Y ranks: 1 to 6 in order, no ties. A tie in X is enough to use the covariance method.

steps.label: (e) Decide the method
steps.text: Scan each column for repeated values. X repeats a value; Y has no repeats. Ties found, so use the covariance method (Pearson on the ranks).

steps.label: (e) Why not d²?
steps.text: With ties the d² formula is only approximate (it would give 0.9714). Give the covariance answer.

steps.label: Putting it together
steps.text: Cov > 0, r = 0.925, b̂ > 0 and r_{s} = 0.971 all say the same thing: a strong positive relationship. r_{s} (0.971) and r (0.925) are close but not identical, because r uses the actual values and r_{s} uses only the order. Correlation shows association, not that study time alone causes the score.

problem.text: Six salespeople were compared on the number of calls made per week (X) and the sales closed in that week, in thousands (Y). Find Spearman's rank correlation coefficient and give your conclusion.

steps.label: Identify
steps.text: Raw values and the words rank correlation: rank each column first.

steps.label: Rank calls (X)
steps.text:
Sort smallest to largest, number the positions 1 to 6, and give a tied value the average of its positions.

| 9 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 12 | 1 | 2 | 2 |
| 15 | 1 | 3 | 3 |
| 18 | 1 | 4 | 4 |
| 22 | 1 | 5 | 5 |
| 30 | 1 | 6 | 6 |
In the original order the ranks are: 3, 5, 1, 6, 4, 2. Check: the ranks add to n(n + 1)/2 = 21; here 21. No value repeats in this column.

steps.label: Decide the method
steps.text: Scan each column for repeated values. X has no repeats; Y has no repeats. No ties, so the d² formula is exact and is all you need.

worked.title: Regression · Predicting beyond the data (study hours, 10 h and 15 h)

problem.text: Using the study-hours data from the All together problem (X = 2, 3, 3, 4, 6, 6 hours; Y = 52, 55, 61, 68, 70, 78) and the fitted line Ŷ = 42.2857 + 5.4286X, predict the exam score (out of 100) for a student who studies 5 hours, 10 hours and 15 hours. Comment on each prediction.

steps.label: Range of the data
steps.text: X runs from 2 to 6 hours. Anything outside that is extrapolation.

steps.label: 5 hours
steps.text: Ŷ = 42.2857 + 5.4286 × 5 = **69.43**. Inside the range, so reliable.

steps.label: 10 hours
steps.text: Ŷ = 42.2857 + 5.4286 × 10 = **96.57**. It is possible, but 10 hours is outside 2 to 6, so this is extrapolation and less reliable.

steps.label: 15 hours
steps.text: Ŷ = 42.2857 + 5.4286 × 15 = **123.71**. A score cannot exceed 100, so this prediction is impossible. The linear model does not hold this far outside the data; the score would level off.

steps.label: What to write
steps.text: Give each number, then: 5 h reliable; 10 h extrapolation, less reliable; 15 h impossible, so the model fails beyond the observed range.

flashcards.back: r = Cov(X, Y) / (s_X · s_Y), with s_X = √Var(X) and s_Y = √Var(Y).
The direction of the linear relationship between two variables. Positive: they move together. Negative: opposite ways. Not the strength.
Cov(X, Y) = E(XY) − E(X)E(Y), where E(XY) = Σ x·y·p(x, y).

flashcards.front: Why is covariance alone not enough?
flashcards.back: Its size changes with the units and has no limits, so it cannot show strength. Only its sign is meaningful.

flashcards.front: The deviations X − X̄ add up to…
flashcards.back: Zero. If they do not, a mean is wrong.

flashcards.front: What is on the diagonal of the variance-covariance matrix?
flashcards.back: The variances. The covariances are off the diagonal, and the matrix is symmetric.
The covariance divided by the product of the two standard deviations. Unit-free, from −1 to +1 (slide 17).
r = [nΣXY − ΣXΣY] / √{[nΣX² − (ΣX)²][nΣY² − (ΣY)²]}.
±1 perfect; ±0.76 to ±0.99 strong; ±0.26 to ±0.75 moderate; 0 to ±0.25 weak; 0 zero.

flashcards.front: What does a negative r mean?
flashcards.back: An inverse relationship: when one variable rises, the other tends to fall.
Something is wrong: r lies between −1 and +1. Recheck ΣX², ΣY² and (ΣX)².
ΣX²: square each value, then add. (ΣX)²: add the values, then square the total.

flashcards.front: Y is a constant. What are Cov and r?
flashcards.back: Cov = 0 but r is undefined (0/0). Say zero covariance, not zero correlation (professor's correction).

flashcards.front: Does a strong r prove causation?
flashcards.back: No. It shows association only.
The covariance between a series at time t + h and at time t, with lag h (slide 13).
γ̂(h) = {{ 1 // n }} Σ (X_{t+|h|} − X̄)(X_{t} − X̄), with the sum over i = 1 to n − |h|. Divide by n.
The sum index should be i, not t (professor, 25 Oct).
The variance of the series (divided by n), since lag 0 pairs each value with itself.
r_{k} = {{ Σ(y_{t} − ȳ)(y_{t−k} − ȳ) // Σ(y_{t} − ȳ)² }} Top: t = k + 1 to T.

flashcards.front: What is PCA in terms of covariance (slides 15–16)?
flashcards.back: Diagonalising the variance-covariance matrix by solving A x = λ x. Large eigenvalue: important component. Near zero: unimportant.

flashcards.front: What do Y and X stand for in regression?
flashcards.back: Y is the dependent (response, predicted) variable. X is the independent (explanatory, predictor) variable.
Y = a + bX + ε. a is the intercept, b is the slope, ε is the error.
b̂ = Σ(X − X̄)(Y − Ȳ) / Σ(X − X̄)²  =  [nΣXY − ΣXΣY] / [nΣX² − (ΣX)²].
â = Ȳ − b̂X̄ and Ŷ = â + b̂X.
ΣY = n·a + b·ΣX and ΣXY = a·ΣX + b·ΣX².

flashcards.front: Which deviations go in the denominator of b̂?
flashcards.back: The X deviations, Σ(X − X̄)². The Showtime slide used the Y deviations by mistake.
The slide gives b̂ = 0.407, which is wrong. The correct values are b̂ = 1.604, â = 88.64, and Ŷ(4.5) = 95.86.

flashcards.front: A quick check on a regression line
flashcards.back: It always passes through (X̄, Ȳ). Predicting at X̄ must give Ȳ.

flashcards.front: How do you know a question is regression?
flashcards.back: "Fit a line", "least squares", "SSE as loss", "predict when X =", "effect of A on B".

flashcards.front: How do you interpret the slope?
flashcards.back: Sign gives the direction. Size gives the change in Y per one unit of X, with units. Then give the prediction.

flashcards.front: Predicting outside the range of the data
flashcards.back: That is extrapolation. Compute it, but add that it is less reliable.
SST = Σ(Y − Ȳ)², SSR = Σ(Ŷ − Ȳ)², SSE = Σ(Y − Ŷ)², and SST = SSR + SSE.
r² = SSR / SST = 1 − SSE / SST. It lies between 0 and 1.
About 87.7% of the variation in Y is explained by the regression on X. The rest is other factors or random variation.
Pearson's r computed on ranks. Add-on topic (May 2026, 5 marks).

flashcards.front: How do you rank tied values?
flashcards.back: Give each tied value the average of the positions they occupy: two values tied for 3rd and 4th both get 3.5.
r_{s} = 1 − 6Σd² / [n(n² − 1)], where d is the difference in ranks. Exact with no ties.

flashcards.front: How often is each CS 11 topic asked?
flashcards.back: Regression fit and predict: 4 of 6 end-sem papers. Pearson r: 4 of 6. Spearman: 1 of 6 (May 2026).

flashcards.front: Regression slope as covariance over variance
flashcards.back: b̂ = Cov(X, Y) / Var(X). The n − 1 cancels, so it equals Σxy / Σx².
r_{s} = 1 − 6Σd² / [n(n² − 1)], with d_i = x_i − y_i the difference of the two ranks.

flashcards.front: How do you decide between the d² formula and the covariance method?
flashcards.back: Scan each column for a repeated value. None: d² formula. A repeat (ties): covariance method on the ranks.
Sort, number the positions, and give tied values the average of their positions. The next value carries on from the last position used.

flashcards.front: Three values tie at positions 2, 3 and 4. What rank does each get?
flashcards.back: 3, the average of 2, 3 and 4. The next value is rank 5; rank 4 is not used.

flashcards.front: Are ties between a value in X and the same value in Y a problem?
flashcards.back: No. Ties are repeats inside one column only.

flashcards.front: Quick check on a list of ranks
flashcards.back: They add to n(n + 1)/2. For n = 6 the ranks add to 21.
Raw measurements with Karl Pearson, linear relation or correlation coefficient: Pearson. Ranks, or the words rank correlation: Spearman.

flashcards.front: Marks given, question says only "correlation coefficient"
flashcards.back: Pearson r. Spearman only if it says rank correlation (then rank the marks first).

flashcards.front: The prediction is at an X outside the data range. What do you write?
flashcards.back: Give the number, then say X is outside the observed range, so the prediction is less reliable.

flashcards.front: The predicted Y is impossible (for example a score above 100). What do you write?
flashcards.back: Say the line predicts it but it is impossible, so the linear model does not hold that far outside the data; the relationship would level off.

quiz.q: Covariance between two variables is positive. This means…
options: X and Y tend to move in the same direction
quiz.explain: A positive covariance gives direction only: same direction. It says nothing about strength or cause.

quiz.q: Why is covariance a poor measure of strength?
options: Its size depends on the units of measurement
quiz.explain: Change kg to grams and the covariance changes. That is why Pearson's r divides by both standard deviations.

quiz.q: Find the covariance of X = 2, 4, 6 and Y = 1, 3, 8.
quiz.explain: X̄ = 4, Ȳ = 4. Products 6, 0, 8 sum to 14. Divide by n − 1 = 2: 7.

quiz.q: Find the covariance of X = 5, 4, 7, 10, 8, 8 and Y = 20, 18, 23, 32, 26, 25 (slides 10–11).
quiz.explain: Sum of products 53, n − 1 = 5, so 10.6.

quiz.q: If X and Y are independent, then…
quiz.explain: E(XY) = E(X)E(Y) when they are independent, so the covariance is 0. The reverse need not hold.

quiz.q: Y is always equal to the same constant K. Which is correct?
quiz.explain: Cov = 0, but sY = 0 so r = 0/0 is undefined (professor's correction to the slide).

quiz.q: Sample covariance of data uses which divisor?
quiz.explain: Slide 8: divide by n − 1.

quiz.q: Pearson's r always lies between…
quiz.explain: r is unit-free and bounded: −1 ≤ r ≤ +1.

quiz.q: r = −0.82 is described as…
quiz.explain: Slide 22: −0.99 to −0.76 is strong negative.

quiz.q: r = 0.4 is described as…
quiz.explain: Slide 22: 0.26 to 0.75 is moderate (intermediate).
All points lie on Y = X + 1, a perfect line: r = +1.
Numerator 5(35) − 15(15) = −50. Both brackets are 50. r = −1.

quiz.q: Sums: n = 5, ΣX = 56, ΣY = 68, ΣXY = 826, ΣX² = 696, ΣY² = 986 (2024 end-sem). Find r.
Sums: n = 6, ΣX = 32, ΣY = 32, ΣXY = 129, ΣX² = 230, ΣY² = 204 (slide 27). Find r.

quiz.explain: r cannot exceed 1. Recheck the sums.

quiz.q: Series 4, 6, 5, 7, 8. Find the sample autocovariance γ̂(0) using the slide formula.
quiz.explain: Mean 6, deviations squared sum to 10, divided by n = 5: 2.

quiz.explain: Products 0, 0, −1, 2 sum to 1; divide by n = 5: 0.2.

quiz.explain: Numerator 1, denominator 10: 0.1.

quiz.q: The sample autocovariance on slide 14 divides the sum by…
quiz.explain: Slide 14: (1/n).

quiz.q: γ̂(0), the autocovariance at lag 0, equals…
quiz.explain: Lag 0 pairs each value with itself, which gives the variance.

quiz.q: In PCA, an eigenvalue near zero means the matching component is…
quiz.explain: Slide 16: a near-zero eigenvalue means the component is relatively unimportant.

quiz.q: "The scores of 5 students in Mathematics (X) and Statistics (Y) are given. Calculate Karl Pearson's coefficient and interpret your result." What do you compute?
options: Regression line of Y on X
Pearson's r, then a sentence on strength and direction

quiz.q: "A company wishes to study the effect of extraction time on efficiency. Fit a straight line by least squares and predict efficiency at 35 minutes." Which is X?
options: Efficiency, because it is the result
Extraction time, because it is the input used to predict
Either, the line is the same

quiz.explain: Coefficient of determination and variation explained point to r² = SSR/SST (slide 55).

quiz.q: "Two judges ranked 6 products. Find the rank correlation coefficient and give your conclusion." What is it?
quiz.explain: Ranks given and the words rank correlation mean Spearman (May 2026 Q4).

quiz.q: "The joint probabilities of X and Y are given in a table. Find Cov(X, Y)." Which formula?
options: Σ(X − X̄)(Y − Ȳ) divided by n − 1
quiz.explain: A probability table means the expectation form (slide 12).

quiz.q: "An IoT system records the temperature on 10 days. Compute the lag-1 autocorrelation and comment on persistence." What is the data shape?
options: One column over time, compared with itself shifted by one step
quiz.explain: One series over time with the word lag: autocorrelation (Mar 2026 Q4).

quiz.q: "Check whether x and y have a linear relation. Find a linear relation using SSE as the loss. Predict y when x is 20." What is the best set of tasks?

blocks.text: The size depends on units. Only the sign is meaningful. For strength, use r.

families.label: Pearson r
families.title: Pearson's r: how strong is the straight-line relationship?
families.lead: Five sums, one formula, then a sentence.

blocks.text: How to recognise it

items: "Karl Pearson", "coefficient of correlation", "strength and direction", "interpret your result".
Two columns of numbers and no request to predict (if they say predict or fit a line, that is regression).
n, X̄, Ȳ.
Deviations X − X̄ and Y − Ȳ.
Var(X) and Var(Y) with the same n − 1, then s_{X} and s_{Y}.
r = Cov(X, Y) / (s_{X} · s_{Y}).
Optional check with the sums form (slides 23–27).
Interpret with the slide 22 table: sign for direction, size for strength.

blocks.label: Write this line
blocks.text: "r = 0.99, a strong positive correlation, so students who score high in one subject also score high in the other. Correlation does not imply causation."

families.label: Autocorrelation
families.title: Autocovariance and autocorrelation: a series against its own past
families.lead: Same idea as covariance, but the second variable is the same series shifted by the lag.

blocks.text: How to recognise it

items: One column of values over time, and the words "lag", "autocovariance" or "autocorrelation".
Mean of the whole series.
Deviations.
Pair each deviation with the one h places later; multiply and add (n − h products).
Divide by n for γ̂(h), or by the sum of squared deviations for r_{k}.
Check r_{k} = γ̂(k)/γ̂(0).

blocks.label: Common mistake
blocks.text: Dividing the autocovariance by n − 1, or forgetting that there are only n − h pairs at lag h.

families.label: Regression
families.title: Regression: fit the line, then use it
families.lead: Fit by least squares, predict, interpret, and answer the judgement parts.

blocks.text: How to recognise it

items: "Fit a line", "least squares", "SSE as the loss", "simple regression", "find a suitable linear relation".
"Predict … when X = …", "effect of A on B", "based on", "Y = f(X)".
Often with extras: interpret the sign, draw a scatter plot, say whether the model is appropriate.

blocks.text: b̂ = {{ Cov(X, Y) // Var(X) }}  =  {{ Σ(X − X̄)(Y − Ȳ) // Σ(X − X̄)² }}  =  {{ nΣXY − (ΣX)(ΣY) // nΣX² − (ΣX)² }}        â = Ȳ − b̂·X̄        Ŷ = â + b̂·X

items: X and Y.
n, X̄, Ȳ.
Deviations x and y (each adds to 0).
Σxy and Σx².
b̂ = Σxy / Σx² (X deviations in the denominator).
â = Ȳ − b̂X̄.
Line, then prediction.
One sentence: direction, size with units, prediction.

blocks.label: Common mistakes
blocks.text: Y deviations in the denominator (the Showtime slide's slip). Swapping X and Y. Extrapolating without a warning. Forgetting units in the sentence.

families.label: r²
families.title: r²: how good is the fitted line?
families.lead: The share of the variation in Y that the line explains.

blocks.text: How to recognise it

items: "coefficient of determination", "variation explained", "how good is the fit", or SSE and SST given.

blocks.text: r² = {{ SSR // SST }} = 1 − {{ SSE // SST }}        SST = SSR + SSE

items: Fit the line and get Ŷ.
SST = Σ(Y − Ȳ)², SSR = Σ(Ŷ − Ȳ)².
r² = SSR / SST.
Say it as a percentage of the variation in Y.

blocks.label: Add-on
blocks.text: r = + or − √r², with the sign of the slope.

families.label: Spearman
families.title: Spearman: correlation of ranks
families.lead: Add-on topic. Pearson's r on the ranks, with averaged ranks for ties.

blocks.text: How to recognise it

items: The data are ranks, or the question says "rank correlation" or "Spearman".
Raw values? Rank each column (smallest = 1), averaging tied positions.
Scan each column for a repeat. **No repeats:** use r_{s} = 1 − 6Σd² / [n(n² − 1)]. **Repeats:** use Cov(rank X, rank Y) / (s_{X}·s_{Y}).
Table, then the formula, then a conclusion on sign and strength.

blocks.text:
r_{s} = 1 − {{ 6 Σd² // n(n² − 1) }}      (no ties)

r_{s} = {{ Cov(rank X, rank Y) // s_{X} · s_{Y} }}      (ties, or always)

blocks.label: Common mistakes
blocks.text: Forgetting to average ties. Using d² when ties exist. Ranking the two columns in opposite directions. Dropping the conclusion sentence.

families.label: All together
families.title: One problem, every Chapter 11 tool
families.lead: Cov, r, regression, r², Spearman on the same data. Work it top to bottom.

blocks.text: Order to work in

items: Table of deviations once; reuse it for Cov, r, the slope and SST.
Cov, then Var(X), Var(Y), then r = Cov / (s_{X}·s_{Y}).
Slope b̂ = Cov / Var(X), intercept â = Ȳ − b̂X̄, predict, interpret.
Fitted values, then SSR, SST, r².
Rank both columns (average ties), then choose d² or the covariance method.

blocks.label: Consistency check
blocks.text: All four measures should agree on the sign. r² = r². Spearman is close to r when the relationship is steady.
